title: Lahaina Disaster Recovery Update Meeting: January 24, 2024

issues.title: Moving fire survivors off FEMA interim housing
Bill 105 rebuilding nonconforming structures after disasters

recap.headline: Lahaina recovery update: debris removal, expedited permits, housing and sewer
recap.in_60_seconds: County, state and federal agencies gave their weekly Lahaina wildfire recovery update in Lahaina. The Mayor said a burned 89-unit Kupuohi affordable housing project will start rebuilding next week after cleaning its own site. The Army Corps of Engineers has finished 10 properties and plans to grow from 7 to about 15 cleanup crews by the end of next week. The County reported 1,934 right-of-entry forms started and 970 processed. Eight residents asked questions about expedited building permits, housing sites, shoreline setbacks, rising rents and the long-awaited Wahikuli sewer line. Funding and timing for the Wahikuli sewer, rules for landlords ending leases, and drinking water at a West Side distribution site were left unresolved.

parts.title: Opening and Kupuohi housing rebuild
presented: Thanked the community and federal partners for Saturday's Unity rally, which included five voyaging canoes.
The burned Kupuohi project, about 89 family units, will begin rebuilding next week, with a goal of finishing within 24 months.
The project cleaned its site at its own expense, met Department of Health requirements and may take debris to the Central Maui Landfill.
The advisory team will run the entire agenda next Wednesday, January 31.

next.what: Mayor's Lahaina Advisory Team leads the meeting and takes questions

parts.title: Lahaina Advisory Team member update
parts.presenter: Lahaina Advisory Team member (health and social services)
presented: She is working with aging services and senior centers to find a place for kūpuna activities and respite for caregivers.
She encouraged people to use the Maui Recovers app for services, especially mental health.
She suggested fire survivors photograph their properties before debris removal.

parts.title: FEMA update
presented: Another right-of-entry meeting with Army Corps experts is set for Saturday, January 27.
About 1,130 recipients have been placed in housing, and that number is growing; survivors offered a unit should take it.
More than 3,000 survivors have received rental assistance, and continued assistance is available through the Disaster Recovery Center.
Insurance additional living expense coverage must be used up first; people should contact FEMA 30 to 45 days before it runs out.

parts.title: Army Corps of Engineers debris removal update
presented: Crews grew from 5 to 7 today; 10 properties are done and 7 more are underway, with about 9 crews expected early next week and about 15 by the end of next week.
Properties next to occupied homes are cleared first; a new public online viewer shows each property's status by color.
The 72-hour call means work will not start sooner than 72 hours; homeowners are welcome to watch with a safety officer.
Wrapped debris is meant to open at the temporary storage site, and wet methods and air monitors are working as intended.

parts.title: EPA sewer line inspection plan
parts.presenter: EPA incident commander for water and wastewater
presented: EPA will inspect about 99,000 linear feet of Lahaina sewer lines starting the first week of February for the Department of Environmental Management.
Crews will flush lines with high-pressure water and send robotic cameras through them so the County can find urgent repairs.
Occupied homes get a door hanger at least 48 hours ahead, and work happens within five days after that.
Wahikuli sewer service is a longer-term recovery issue being handled by the County Office of Recovery, the Department of Health, EPA and congressional staff.

parts.title: County right-of-entry update
parts.presenter: County of Maui Department of Management staff
presented: 1,934 right-of-entry forms have been started; the Mayor later corrected the number processed and sent to the Army Corps to 970.
About 85% of residential and 44% of commercial forms have been received.
Applicants must verify their email address to submit; help is available at 808-727-1515.
Workshop at the Lahainaluna High School cafeteria this Saturday from 3 to 5:30 p.m.

next.what: Right-of-entry workshop at Lahainaluna High School cafeteria

parts.title: Air and water monitoring, and SBA loan deadline
parts.presenter: Department of Health deputy director for environmental health; SBA public information officer
presented: There are 37 purple air sensors in and around Lahaina and 3 in Olowalu; 7 more were installed today, and residents with power and Wi-Fi can host one.
Results of air sampling for heavy metals and asbestos are expected in early February; results of nearshore water sampling will take two to three months.
Air quality can be checked at fire.airnow.gov.
Tomorrow is the last day to apply for an SBA disaster loan, which is open to homeowners, renters, nonprofits and businesses; help line 1-800-659-2955.

next.what: Heavy metals and asbestos air results

parts.title: Office of Recovery public sentiment analysis
parts.presenter: County Managing Director, Office of Recovery
presented: Testimony from past meetings was grouped into nine themes, including community voice, housing and jobs, culture, resilient infrastructure, water rights, green space and trauma-informed leadership.
The recovery support teams use the West Maui Community Plan as a foundation.
Not every request can be done, and some community requests conflict with each other.
More formal engagement, such as town halls, is likely in February.

next.what: Formal community engagement sessions on recovery

parts.title: Council member remarks
presented: She encouraged people to do whatever helps them heal and said strong emotions and being easily startled are natural responses to trauma.
She thanked first responders and County workers, many of whom lost their own homes.

parts.title: Questions from the audience and closing
presented: The moderator opened the floor to questions and said the advisory team will lead next week.

raised.concern: Whether building permits are being processed for rebuilding.
The community hears about housing sites such as Launiupoko and Kāʻanapali modular units from outside sources and wants a say in where they go.
When the Wahikuli area will get sewer service, and whether sewer lines can be installed now before homes are rebuilt so owners do not pay for septic systems and then again to connect.
Whether a disaster emergency building permit provision, code section 105.2.1, can be used.
Whether generational Hawaiian families can rebuild homes on Front Street within the 120-foot shoreline setback.
Lack of drinking water at the West Side distribution center and no follow-up on getting a water tank there.
Families housed in Red Cross condos are being moved again into hotels without kitchens.
Long-term renters are losing their leases as landlords take higher FEMA-paid rents, and they want regulation.

answered.said: An expedited permitting office is being set up. Bids from outside firms are being reviewed, with a selection hoped for by February 16, and a council committee hears the first steps tomorrow. It covers only single-family homes and accessory units, about 1,200 properties.
The goal is first reviews within 15 days by an outside firm. Expedited review would also cover Kula and survivors rebuilding on other property they own on Maui.

Interim housing sites are picked for speed and existing infrastructure, without polling the community on each site. Launiupoko is a State project; long-term sites could be discussed with the community later with HUD funding.
No area can be assessed until cameras run through the lines; the short-term goal is restoring service, and bigger repairs may come later.
National building code provisions are being matched with state and county requirements as the expedited process is designed.
There is no firm answer yet; shoreline rules did not foresee a whole town being lost, and this will be a key topic in community engagement.
Contracts for those condos are between the Red Cross and the State, some owners set limited availability, and the goal is longer-term interim housing.
He did not understand the water question and asked whether it meant cases or pallets of water.

Early lease endings are an unintended result of FEMA paying short-term rental rates. The administration supports a legislative bill to cap rents on Maui, the governor's proclamation bars evictions, FEMA has reached about 1,300 units, and owners who do not join will face higher taxes.
Hard blue rock makes a Wahikuli sewer very costly. The treatment plant has capacity, construction would take at least a year after design, and designs have been sent to FEMA and EPA.
The County is seeking federal, state and philanthropic funds; EPA has not said no, and costs to owners cannot be answered tonight.

next.what: Council committee hears first steps of expedited permitting
Maui rent cap bill introduced at the Legislature

bills.name: Expedited permitting proposal
bills.what: Sets up a faster permit review for rebuilding single-family homes and accessory units, using an outside firm.

bills.name: State rent cap bill for Maui
bills.what: A bill at the Legislature that would set a rent ceiling only for Maui.

bills.name: Governor's emergency proclamation
bills.what: Bars evictions during the emergency, with an exception for owners' family members moving in.

bills.name: West Maui Community Plan
bills.what: Used as the foundation for the recovery support teams' strategies.

bills.name: International Building Code section 105.2.1
bills.what: A disaster emergency building permit provision a resident asked about.

open_questions.question: When and how will Wahikuli get sewer lines, and who will pay?
Will drinking water tanks be provided at the West Side distribution center?
Can generational Hawaiian families rebuild within the 120-foot shoreline setback on Front Street?
How will the community have a say in where interim and permanent housing is built?

not_on_tracker.topic: Army Corps debris removal and right-of-entry progress
not_on_tracker.why: Property owners need cleanup finished before they can rebuild.

not_on_tracker.topic: Rising rents and lease endings tied to FEMA housing payments

moments.who: County Managing Director helping lead the Office of Recovery
moments.quote: So, in the coming weeks ahead, likely sometime in February, we're going to be getting on kind of more formal community engagement processes. What that could look like is public comment sessions where we'll have possible town hall meetings or separate sessions to provide feedback
moments.about: Gives the expected timing and format for formal community input on the recovery planning process.

moments.quote: FEMA can only assist us for a certain period. The next thing that's going to happen, our more permanent is going to be HUD. HUD's going to come in and help us. We made a request for $1.2 billion from HUD to help us rebuild Lahaina.
moments.about: Shows the early county request for HUD disaster recovery money to rebuild Lahaina, the start of the federal recovery grant.

moments.who: A Lahaina resident living on Hawaiian Home Lands
moments.quote: We can rebuild within the 120 setback for the generational Hawaiian homes that were on the beaches on Front Street. It's our just hope. Because right now under the setback laws and the destruction, 100% destruction, I can't build anything within 120 feet of the shoreline.
moments.about: Shows how shoreline setback rules affect families hoping to rebuild generational homes on Front Street, a question officials said is a hot topic for recovery planning.
